To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we: 1) propose a novel multi-task network architecture for off-axis eye gaze estimation and user understanding, 2) propose a novel dataset of 587 eye images with 4.6K eye annotations, and 3) show that our model trained on MagicEyes outperforms the state-of-the-art on all tasks by large margins.

EyeNet: 1) outperforms the state-of-the-art on pupil/cornea estimation, eye segmentation, blink and expression classification and 2) is the first work to address off-axis eye gaze and semantic user understanding in a single deep learning framework.
In summary, our research is concerned with

i) a new dataset of 3.5 million images of eyes with 587 subjects and 5 imaging conditions; ii) a new single network that jointly solves eye segmentation, blink, emotion, glints detection and eye gaze estimation; iii) the first work to estimate gaze in off-axis images; iv) a new model based loss function for eye segmentation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our network is the first to achieve state-of-the-art performance for all eye gaze related tasks in off-axis imaging.

the presented method achieves the state-of-the-art in pupil and cornea detection, eye segmentation, and blink detection, while being the first to address the problem of emotive expression classification and IR glints detection.
EyeNet is the first deep network which can solve multiple eye related tasks simultaneously for off-axis eye images.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
EyeNet outperforms all previous methods in all tasks, and is also the first method that solves the challenging problem of off-axis pupil/cornea center estimation.
EyeNet achieves state of the art performance for all tasks on the MagicEyes dataset and outperforms the state of the art on the MPIIGaze dataset.
we present a single network which solves multiple related tasks and outperforms the state-of-the-art on each of them.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a single network can be used to solve all these tasks, which are typically addressed with separate models, with high performance.
the tasks are complementary to each other, with one task improving the performance of other.
a single network can learn all tasks simultaneously with minimal supervision, achieving state-of-the-art results on all tasks.
